This Quarto file contains all the code used for the study titled "The
impact of the two-child benefit cap on parental mental, general, and
financial health in the UK", currently available as a preprint on
[MedRXiv](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.03.30.26349774v1.full).
This code is divided into four sections: sections 1 and 2 deal with
merging and data prep for code from waves 1-14 (2009-2023) of UKHLS
data, while section 3 is related to imputation, and section 4 is the
analysis section.



# Section 1: merging USOC data files

This section of the code retrieves variables from multiple code files
and creates a dataset that will then be edited/prepared in Section 2-3
and analysed in Section 4.

## Setup

Clearing all old objects if present, then installing and loading
packages. Working directory is not set because this runs inside an
`.Rproj` file.

```{r}
#| label: clear-objects
# clearing all old objects if present
rm(list = ls())
```

```{r}
#| label: install-load-packages
# installing and loading package(s) needed
install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
#| label: set-paths-and-waves
# not setting wd because I am working in an .Rproj file

# setting directory for data retrieval from folder in .Rproj file
ukhls <- "UKDA-6614-tab/tab/ukhls" 

# naming file produced at the end of this (change as updated)
outputfilename <- "20251210_UKHLS_total"

# setting "allWaves", which will be called below
allWaves <- letters[1:14]  # waves a-n, corresponding to waves 1-14 of UKHLS
```

## Retrieving variables

Where possible, retrieving variables ending in `_dv`, as those have been
derived from one or more sources in UKHLS and are therefore (possibly)
more accurate.

### Household-level variables (`hhresp`)

List of variables retrieved from this file:

`hidp` - household ID

`hhsize` - household size

`fihhmnnet1_dv` - total net household income (no deductions),
derived net monthly

`ieqmoecd_dv` - modified OECD equivalence scale

`agechy_dv` - age of youngest child, derived

```{r}
#| label: hhvars
# retrieving variables from "hhresp".tab - household-level response file
hhvars <- c("hidp", "hhsize", "fihhmnnet1_dv", "ieqmoecd_dv", "agechy_dv")
```

### Individual / adult response variables (`indresp`, age 16+)

Note: I would have included `ukborn`, but it was a proxy variable, so
I'll be retrieving it during the data cleaning step from the `xwavedat`
file.

List of variables retrieved from this file:

`pidp` - person ID

`hidp` - household ID

`intdaty_dv` - interview date year, derived

`intdatm_dv` - interview date month, derived

`ioutcome` - interview outcome (for filtering to productive
interviews)

`ivfio` - interview type (to filter out proxies)

`ethn_dv` - ethnicity, derived (note that I would have included
`ukborn` here, but it was a proxy variable, so I'll be retrieving it
during the data cleaning step from xwavedat file)

`single_dv` - whether single in household

`scghq`(a-l) - GHQ question variables

`sf1` - Wave 1 self-rated health measure

`scsf`(1-7) - SF-12 measures

`hiqual_dv` - highest educational qualification ever reported

`jbnssec3_dv` - current NS-SEC occupation class, derived (3 class
version)

`mastat_dv` - de facto marital status, derived

`hcond`(1-16, 18-19, 21, 23-24, 26-29) - health conditions

`disdif`(1-12) - disability questions

`health` - long-standing health variable, not used for the variable

`oprlg1` - religion

`sclfsat1` - health satisfaction outcome measure

`sclfsato` - overall life satisfaction outcome measure

`finnow` - current financial situation, subjective rating

`finfut` - future financial situation, subjective rating

`urban_dv` - urban vs rural identification, derived

`ff_ivlolw` - fed forward interview outcome prev wave

`ff_everint` - fed forward ever interviewed

```{r}
             "hcond1", "hcond2", "hcond3", "hcond4", "hcond5", "hcond6", 
             "hcond7", "hcond8", "hcond9", "hcond10", "hcond11", "hcond12",
```

### Household enumeration variables (`indall`)

List of variables retrieved from this file:

**`pidp`** - person ID

**`hidp`** - household ID

**`age_dv`** - age in completed years at time of interview, derived

**`sex_dv`** - sex, derived

**`doby_dv`** - date of birth year, derived

```{r}
#| label: indallvars
# retrieving variables from "indall".tab - enumeration of all household members
indallvars <- c("pidp", "hidp", "age_dv", "sex_dv", "doby_dv")
```

## Merging variables: R-native approach

Now that you have the retrieved variables, this section reads all waves
of each file type, then merges them, by reading a file from each wave
and adding a wave indicator.

```{r}
#| label: read-wave-file
# helper function to read a wave file and add wave indicator
read_wave_file <- function(wave, filename, vars_to_keep) {
  filepath <- file.path(ukhls, paste0(wave, "_", filename, ".tab"))
  
  if (!file.exists(filepath)) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # first read just column names to see what exists
  col_names <- names(read_tsv(filepath, n_max = 0, show_col_types = FALSE))
  
  # checking for both prefixed and non-prefixed versions of variables
  wave_vars <- paste0(wave, "_", vars_to_keep)  # e.g., "a_hidp"
  no_prefix_vars <- vars_to_keep  # e.g., "pidp"
  
  # keeping variables that exist (either with or without prefix)
  existing_vars <- c(wave_vars[wave_vars %in% col_names], 
                     no_prefix_vars[no_prefix_vars %in% col_names])
  
  if (length(existing_vars) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # reading only those columns
  df <- read_tsv(filepath, col_select = all_of(existing_vars), show_col_types = FALSE)
  
  # removing wave prefix from variables that have it
  names(df) <- gsub(paste0("^", wave, "_"), "", names(df))
  
  # adding wave indicator
  df$wavename <- which(letters == wave)
  
  return(df)
}
```

### Reading and appending `hhresp` files (household level)

```{r}
#| label: read-hhresp
# reading and appending files, by type
# HHRESP files (household level)
hhresp_list <- map(allWaves, ~read_wave_file(.x, "hhresp", hhvars))
hhresp_all <- bind_rows(hhresp_list)
# "hhresp_all" has 319615 obs of 6 vars
```

### Reading and appending `indresp` files (adult responses)

```{r}
#| label: read-indresp
# INDRESP files (adult responses)
indresp_list <- map(allWaves, ~read_wave_file(.x, "indresp", indvars))
indresp_all <- bind_rows(indresp_list)
# "indresp_all" has 568946 obs of 84 vars
```

### Merging `hhresp` and `indresp`

Merging everything together, faithful to Jen Dykxhoorn's approach.
Starting with `hhresp` (household level), then merging `indresp` by
`hidp` and `wavename`.

```{r}
#| label: merge-hh-ind
# merging everything together
# starting with hhresp (household level)
df_final <- hhresp_all

# merging indresp by hidp and wavename
df_final <- df_final %>%
  left_join(indresp_all, by = c("hidp", "wavename"), suffix = c("_hh", ""))
```

### Reading and appending `indall` files (all individuals, including children)

```{r}
#| label: read-indall
# INDALL files (all individuals - for household enumeration)
indall_list <- map(allWaves, ~read_wave_file(.x, "indall", indallvars))
indall_all <- bind_rows(indall_list)
# "indall_all" has 824224 obs of 6 vars
```

### Merging `indall` into main file

```{r}
#| label: merge-indall
# merging indall to get all household members (including children)
df_final <- df_final %>%
  left_join(indall_all, by = c("hidp", "wavename", "pidp"), suffix = c("", "_indall"))
# "df_final" has 564091 obs of 91 vars
```

### Filter to productive interviews (excluding proxies)

This is done specifically to narrow down the sample to interviews that
happened, therefore which will have results.

```{r}
#| label: filter-productive
# filtering to productive interviews, excluding proxies
df_final <- df_final %>%
  filter(ioutcome %in% c(11, 21)) %>%  # full productive and partial productive interviews
  filter(ivfio != 2 | is.na(ivfio))    # exclude proxy respondents
# "df_final" has 532834 obs of 91 vars
```

### Reorder ID columns

This is for my own sake, to have the ID files at the beginning for
viewing purposes.

```{r}
#| label: reorder-cols
# move pidp and hidp to the beginning of the file
df_final <- df_final %>% select(pidp, hidp, wavename, everything())
```

### Saving outputs

In this case, saving both the long file and the environment in case
other files in the creation of the long file are needed.

```{r}
#| label: save-outputs
# saving the long file
saveRDS(df_final, paste0(outputfilename, ".rds"))

# saving environment 
save.image("20251210_environment.RData")
```

# Section 2: cleaning the USOC data file

The purpose of this to clean the USOC data file, merged above from
Section 1.

It uses output from the above file as input, but should also add
environment saved from that file too. If the entire environment is
needed (which it is if you haven't run the merge code before this), load
this code:

```{r}
#| label: load-environment
load("20251202_environment.RData")
```

If you've just started by running only this section, you can load this
chunk of packages needed.

```{r}
#| label: install-load-packages-2
# installing and loading package(s) needed
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("data.table")
install.packages("zoo")
library(data.table) # load first because this code uses tidyverse more
library(tidyverse) # will already have been loaded if R-native merge code was run right before this, but adding here for if needed
library(zoo)
```

**Sample selection criteria:** individuals with at least one child 5 or
under, one household respondent, at least one question in GHQ-12.

```{r}
#| label: import-data
# import in data file from USOC merge code file
UKHLS_total <- readRDS("20251210_UKHLS_total.rds")
# "UKHLS_total" has 532834 obs of 91 vars
```

```{r}
#| label: init-clean
# creating new clean dataset to work with
UKHLS_clean <- data.frame()
```

## Time and linking structures

First, I inspected the interview years for missingness and checking Ns
of those.

```{r}
#| label: time-inspect
# checking interview year
table(UKHLS_total$intdaty_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 4 people with missing year and 922 people in year 2024 -- will need to filter out based on interview year, if not known, then will not be able to assign a before/after condition
table(UKHLS_total$intdatm_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 4 people with missing month
```

### Building clean time variables (`intyear`, `intmonth`, `intym`)

Based on the results above, then doing the following:

-   Filtering out those with year(s) after 2023 for now to keep
    interview year consistent with the 2009–2023 time window of interest
    (but can add them back in though once Wave 15 is out).
-   Renaming `intdaty_dv` to `intyear` for ease, and selecting relevant
    anchoring variables: `pidp` (person ID), `hidp` (household ID),
    `wavename` (even though we will be using year for analysis, having
    the wavename increases consistency for linking), and `intyear`.
-   Creating an `intym` variable for interview year-month combination
    (it's a character variable but you can apparently still sort on it
    properly).

```{r}
#| label: time-clean
UKHLS_clean <- UKHLS_total %>%
  rename(intyear = intdaty_dv) %>%
  rename(intmonth = intdatm_dv) %>%
  mutate(intyear = case_when(
    intyear == -9 ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(intyear)
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(intyear) & intyear <= 2023) %>%
  mutate(intmonth = case_when(
    intmonth == -9 ~ NA_real_, # missing
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(intmonth)
  )) %>%
  mutate(intym = paste0(intyear, "-", str_pad(intmonth, 2, pad = "0"))) %>% # making sure NA doesn't break this step
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, intmonth, intyear, intym) 
# "UKHLS_clean" has 531908 obs of 6 vars
```

### Sense-checking time variable missingness

```{r}
#| label: time-check
# sense-checking intyear, intmonth, intym and wavename vars before proceeding
table(UKHLS_clean$intyear, useNA = "ifany") # no missing
table(UKHLS_clean$intmonth, useNA = "ifany") # no missing
table(UKHLS_clean$intym, useNA = "ifany") # no missing
table(UKHLS_clean$wavename, UKHLS_clean$intyear, useNA = "ifany") # no missing
# seems like it visually makes sense
```

## Exposure variables

This section creates the family variables, identifying parents and
children, as well as creating exposure variables. I first start by
retrieving `indall` files as needed to get all household members
(including children); these should already be loaded but if not, go back
and load the entire environment.

### Number of children under 18 (if needed)

```{r}
#| label: children-u18
# number of children under 18
children_u18 <- indall_all %>%
  filter(age_dv >= 0 & age_dv < 18) %>%
  group_by(hidp, wavename) %>%
  summarise(n_children_u18 = n(), .groups = "drop")
# "children_u18" contains 104327 obs of 3 vars
```

### Number of children aged 5 or under

This will be the pool I am using to identify parents from the individual
dataset later on.

```{r}
#| label: children-5-under
# number of children 5 or under
children_5_under <- indall_all %>%
  filter(age_dv >= 0 & age_dv <= 5) %>%
  group_by(hidp, wavename) %>%
  summarise(n_children_5_under = n(), .groups = "drop")
# "children_5_under" contains 43982 obs of 3 vars
```

### Third-or-later child birth-order info

Checking if any 3rd or later child was born post-policy (2017 or later),
AND capturing the birth year of the 3rd child specifically. The reason
this matters is because, if the 3rd child is born after the policy, the
family will be considered "affected", but if the 3rd child was born
before, then the family still receives money for three children.

```{r}
#| label: third-plus-child-info
third_plus_child_info <- indall_all %>%
  filter(age_dv >= 0) %>%
  group_by(hidp, wavename) %>%
  arrange(desc(age_dv)) %>%  # oldest to youngest
  mutate(birth_order = row_number()) %>%
  summarise(
    # birth year of specifically the 3rd child (for exclusion of 2017 births)
    third_child_yob = doby_dv[birth_order == 3][1],
    # whether ANY 3rd+ child was born 2017 or later (for treatment assignment)
    any_third_plus_post_policy = as.numeric(any(doby_dv[birth_order >= 3] >= 2017, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
# "third_plus_child_info" contains 327152 obs of 4 vars
```

### Merging child counts and third-child info into clean dataset

```{r}
#| label: merge-child-info
# merging child counts, third+ child info, and age of youngest child into UKHLS_clean
UKHLS_clean <- UKHLS_clean %>%
  left_join(children_u18, by = c("hidp", "wavename")) %>%
  left_join(children_5_under, by = c("hidp", "wavename")) %>%
  left_join(third_plus_child_info, by = c("hidp", "wavename")) %>%
  left_join(
    UKHLS_total %>% select(pidp, hidp, wavename, agechy_dv),
    by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename")
  ) %>%
  # replace NAs with 0 for households with no children
  mutate(
    n_children_u18 = replace_na(n_children_u18, 0),
    n_children_5_under = replace_na(n_children_5_under, 0),
    any_third_plus_post_policy = replace_na(any_third_plus_post_policy, 0)
  )
# "UKHLS_clean" contains 531912 obs of 11 vars
```

### Restricting to analytic sample

Filtering the clean dataset to households with at least one child ≤5 AND
valid age data.

```{r}
#| label: analytic-sample
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_clean %>%
  filter(n_children_5_under > 0 & !is.na(agechy_dv) & !agechy_dv %in% c(-8, -9))
```

### Constructing exposure and treatment variables

Using information created from steps above to construct variables which
will be used for analyses below, including:

-   `age_youngest_child`

-   `family_3plus` - binary indicator of whether someone has three or
    more children

-   `treated` - used to distinguish 1-2 children individuals
    specifically from 3+ children individuals *affected by the policy*
    (distinct from unaffected 3+ children individuals)

-   `time_since_policy` - a centered year variable (where 2017 = 0)

-   `time_bucket` - time period indicators for propensity score matching
    later on

```{r}
#| label: treatment-vars
# creating exposure and treatment variables
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  mutate(
    # age of youngest child (no longer needs NA handling since filtered above)
    age_youngest_child = agechy_dv,
    
    # family structure indicators
    family_3plus = ifelse(n_children_u18 >= 3, 1, 0),
    youngest_5_under = ifelse(age_youngest_child <= 5, 1, 0),
    
    # policy timing indicator (April 2017 cutoff)
    post_policy_month = ifelse(intym >= "2017-04", 1, 0),
    
    # treatment group assignment (time-invariant)
    # 0 = control (1-2 children, youngest ≤5)
    # 1 = treated (3+ children, any 3rd+ child born 2017+, youngest ≤5)
    # NA = excluded (unaffected 3+)
    treated = case_when(
      family_3plus == 0 & youngest_5_under == 1 ~ 0,
      family_3plus == 1 & youngest_5_under == 1 & any_third_plus_post_policy == 1 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    
    # time variable centered at policy implementation
    time_since_policy = intyear - 2017,
    
    # time bucket variable for PSM matching
    time_bucket = case_when(
      intyear %in% c(2009:2012) ~ 1,
      intyear %in% c(2013:2016) ~ 2,
      intyear %in% c(2017:2023) ~ 3,
    )
  )
# "UKHLS_analytic" contains 74826 obs of 18 vars
```

## Outcome variables

For ease of interpretation, all directionality of coding will be kept
consistent between variables (so higher scores = worse outcomes).
Outcomes created are in three groups - **mental health** (psychological
distress, life satisfaction), **general health** (HRQoL, self-rated
health, health satisfaction), and **financial health** (financial
situation and financial outlook). I will note that, for consistency's
sake, the labels use the old nomenclature within the code, but you can
use the different headings as indication of the outcomes or refer to the
specific list below:

**Mental health**

-   psychological distress: `GHQ_total`

-   life satisfaction: `life_sat`

**General health**

-   health-related quality of life (HRQoL): `SF_total`

-   self-rated health: `general_health`

-   health satisfaction: `health_sat`

**Financial health**

-   financial situation: `finnow`

-   financial outlook: `finfut`

The first step is filtering the outcomes to clean them:

```{r}
#| label: outcomes-init
outcomes <- UKHLS_total %>%
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, scghqa:scghql, sf1, scsf1:scsf7, sclfsat1, sclfsato, finnow, finfut)
# "outcomes" contains 532834 obs of 32 vars
```

The way this had initially been done, I retrieved the outcomes based on
where they appeared in the USOC dataset, so I am cleaning each outcome
separately.

### Psychological distress (`GHQ_total`)

This measure uses GHQ-12 coding questionnaire data. First, I am checking
values of each GHQ question before changing.

```{r}
#| label: ghq-inspect
# scghqa - concentration
table(outcomes$scghqa, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqb - loss of sleep
table(outcomes$scghqb, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqc - playing a useful role
table(outcomes$scghqc, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqd - capable of making decisions
table(outcomes$scghqd, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqe - constantly under strain
table(outcomes$scghqe, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqf - problem overcoming difficulties
table(outcomes$scghqf, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqg - enjoying day-to-day activities
table(outcomes$scghqg, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqh - ability to face up to problems
table(outcomes$scghqh, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqi - unhappy or depressed
table(outcomes$scghqi, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqj - losing confidence
table(outcomes$scghqj, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghqk - believing worthless
table(outcomes$scghqk, useNA = "ifany") 
# scghql - general happiness
table(outcomes$scghql, useNA = "ifany") 
```

Now I am renaming the dataset variable names for ease of use.

```{r}
#| label: ghq-rename
# now cleaning dataset variables - renaming first for ease of use
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  rename(GHQ_q1 = scghqa,
         GHQ_q2 = scghqb,
         GHQ_q3 = scghqc,
         GHQ_q4 = scghqd,
         GHQ_q5 = scghqe,
         GHQ_q6 = scghqf,
         GHQ_q7 = scghqg,
         GHQ_q8 = scghqh,
         GHQ_q9 = scghqi,
         GHQ_q10 = scghqj,
         GHQ_q11 = scghqk,
         GHQ_q12 = scghql)
```

Now is the recoding: updating each question and scoring `-1` (don't
know), `-2` (refused), `-7` (proxy), `-8` (not applicable) and `-9`
(missing) to NA. All measures are considered "recently" in terms of time
frame.

```{r}
#| label: ghq-recode
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(across(GHQ_q1:GHQ_q12, ~case_when(
    .x %in% c(-9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
    .x == 1 ~ 0,
    .x == 2 ~ 1,
    .x == 3 ~ 2,
    .x == 4 ~ 3,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(.x)
  )))
```

Finally, I ran person-mean imputation in order to substitute missingness
of individual items (since those tend to be MNAR - missing not at
random- we didn't want to exclude people who might have sysmetatically
chosen not to answer certain questions) for the measurements, and then
created a total GHQ measure (0–36) and ran a sense check on the
distribution of values.

```{r}
#| label: ghq-total
# person-mean imputation
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    # calculate person mean across all GHQ items
    person_mean = rowMeans(select(., GHQ_q1:GHQ_q12), na.rm = TRUE),
    # impute missing values with person mean
    across(GHQ_q1:GHQ_q12, ~if_else(is.na(.x), person_mean, .x)),
    # create composite score
    GHQ_total = rowSums(across(GHQ_q1:GHQ_q12))
  ) %>%
  select(-person_mean)
# "outcomes" contains 532834 obs of 33 vars
```

```{r}
#| label: ghq-check

# checking GHQ total distribution
table(outcomes$GHQ_total, useNA = "ifany") # 37104 obs NA
```

### Health-related quality of life (`SF_total`) and self-rated health (`general_health`)

For this measure, I used the composite score of the SF-12 (self-rated
health will be the first question, which I will explain that in a bit).
Similarly to above, I created a score by cleaning and adding each
question's measure.

For SF-12, it doesn't seem like measurements from separate questions are
available for wave 1, so I will have to keep that in mind. I will first
check these separate measures.

```{r}
#| label: sf12-inspect
# scsf1 - question 1 - also general health question
table(outcomes$sf1, useNA = "ifany")
table(outcomes$scsf1, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf2a - health limiting moderate activities
table(outcomes$scsf2a, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf2b - health limiting climbing several flights of stairs

# scsf3a - physical health limits amount of work
table(outcomes$scsf3a, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf3b - physical health limits type of work
table(outcomes$scsf3b, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf4a - mental health meant accomplished less
table(outcomes$scsf4a, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf4b - mental health meant worked less carefully
table(outcomes$scsf4b, useNA = "ifany")
# scsf5 - pain interfered with work

# scsf6b - had a lot of energy

# scsf6c - felt downhearted and depressed

# scsf7 - physical or mental health interfered with social life
table(outcomes$scsf7, useNA = "ifany")
```

**Reverse-coding plan**

I needed to add this because the SF-12 is scored differently
directionally for certain items.

The SF-12 is scored from 1–5, with some higher scores initially
indicating better health, but now will be scored for higher scores to
indicate worse health). Updating each question — numbers will be
reverse-coded, but scoring `-1` (don't know), `-2` (refused), `-7`
(proxy), `-8` (not applicable), `-9` (missing) and `-10` (not available
for IEMB) to NA. All measures "recently" in terms of time frame.

To reverse-score (higher was better, need to flip):

-   Out of 5: 3a, 3b, 4a, 4b, 6c, 7
-   Out of 3: 2a, 2b

To keep same score (higher already = worse):

-   Out of 5: 1, 5, 6a, 6b

**Self-rated health** (`general_health`)

To create this measure, I specifically combined `sf1` (Wave 1) and
`scsf1` (Wave 2+) responses for question 1 of the SF-12. This was done
because, from wave 2 onwards, scsf provides the individual-level
responses to SF-12 questions, while sf1 becomes a proxy measure. That
being said, the specific naming of the variable happens below in the
final outcomes cleaning step.

```{r}
#| label: sf12-general-health
# creating combined general health variable (sf1 from Wave 1, scsf1 from Wave 2+)
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    # cleaning both variables - KEEP
    sf1_clean = case_when(
      sf1 %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(sf1)
    ),
    scsf1_clean = case_when(
      scsf1 %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(scsf1)
    ),
    # combine: using sf1 ONLY for Wave 1, scsf1 for all other waves
    scsf1_combined = case_when(
      wavename == "a" ~ sf1_clean,  # Wave 1 only
      TRUE ~ scsf1_clean  # Wave 2+ use scsf1
    )
  ) %>%
  select(-sf1_clean, -scsf1_clean) # scsf1_combined in SF-12 calculation
```

**Cleaning and reverse-code remaining SF-12 items**

See above list for which variables needed to be coded/recoded, but they
are also present in comments below:

```{r}
#| label: sf12-recode
# cleaning other SF-12 variables
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    # 2a, 2b: REVERSE CODE (1=limited a lot is worse, but coded as 1, need to flip to 3)
    # Original: 1=limited a lot (worst), 3=not limited (best)
    # Want: 3=limited a lot (worst), 1=not limited (best)
    scsf2a = case_when(
      scsf2a %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 4 - as.numeric(scsf2a)  # reverse for 1-3 scale
    ),
    scsf2b = case_when(
      scsf2b %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 4 - as.numeric(scsf2b)  # reverse for 1-3 scale
    ),
    
    # 3a, 3b: REVERSE CODE (1=all the time is worst, need to flip)
    # Original: 1=all the time (worst), 5=none of the time (best)
    # Want: 5=all the time (worst), 1=none of the time (best)
    scsf3a = case_when(
      scsf3a %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf3a)  # reverse-coding
    ),
    scsf3b = case_when(
      scsf3b %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf3b)  # reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 4a, 4b: REVERSE CODE (1=all the time is worst, need to flip)
    scsf4a = case_when(
      scsf4a %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf4a)  # reverse-coding
    ),
    scsf4b = case_when(
      scsf4b %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf4b)  # reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 5: KEEP SAME (1=not at all is best, 5=extremely is worst) - already correct direction
    scsf5 = case_when(
      scsf5 %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(scsf5)  # NO reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 6a: KEEP SAME (1=all the time calm is best, 5=none of the time calm is worst) - already correct direction
    scsf6a = case_when(
      scsf6a %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(scsf6a)  # NO reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 6b: KEEP SAME (1=all the time energy is best, 5=none of the time energy is worst) - already correct direction
    scsf6b = case_when(
      scsf6b %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(scsf6b)  # NO reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 6c: REVERSE CODE (1=all the time depressed is worst, need to flip)
    # Original: 1=all the time (worst), 5=none of the time (best)
    # Want: 5=all the time (worst), 1=none of the time (best)
    scsf6c = case_when(
      scsf6c %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf6c)  # reverse-coding
    ),
    
    # 7: REVERSE CODE (1=all the time interfered is worst, need to flip)
    # Original: 1=all the time (worst), 5=none of the time (best)
    # Want: 5=all the time (worst), 1=none of the time (best)
    scsf7 = case_when(
      scsf7 %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ 6 - as.numeric(scsf7)  # reverse-coding
    )
  )
```

**Person-mean imputation and generation of `SF_total`**

Similar to the psychological distress outcome above, since this is from
a questionnaire, we didn't want to exclude individuals because of
selective non-responses, so we used the same approach here for
person-mean-imputing missing values before creating the total `SF_total`
variable and doing a sense check on the distribution.

```{r}
#| label: sf12-total
# person-mean imputation step for SF-12 
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(
    person_mean = rowMeans(select(., scsf1_combined, scsf2a:scsf7), na.rm = TRUE),
    # impute missing values
    scsf1_combined = if_else(is.na(scsf1_combined), person_mean, scsf1_combined),
    across(scsf2a:scsf7, ~if_else(is.na(.x), person_mean, .x)),
    # create SF total
    SF_total = rowSums(across(c(scsf1_combined, scsf2a:scsf7)))
  ) %>%
  select(-person_mean)
# "outcomes" contains 532834 obs of 35 vars
```

```{r}
#| label: sf12-check
# checking SF total distribution
table(outcomes$SF_total, useNA = "ifany") # 76384 obs NA
```

### Health satisfaction (`health_sat`)

Scale is 1–7, with 1 initially being "completely dissatisfied" and 7
being "completely satisfied". Now switching to 1 = "completely
satisfied" and 7 = "completely dissatisfied". Setting `-1` (don't know),
`-2` (refused), `-7` (proxy), `-8` (not applicable), `-9` (missing),
`-10` (not available for IEMB) to NA.

```{r}
#| label: health-sat
# health satisfaction
# first, checking values of health satisfaction measure before changing
table(outcomes$sclfsat1, useNA = "ifany")
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  rename(health_sat = sclfsat1) %>%
  mutate(health_sat = case_when(
    health_sat %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ 8 - as.numeric(health_sat)) # reverse-coding
  )
table(outcomes$health_sat, useNA = "ifany") # 42831 missing
```

### Life satisfaction (`life_sat`)

1–7 scale, with 1 initially being "completely dissatisfied" and 7 being
"completely satisfied". Now switching to 1 = "completely satisfied" and
7 = "completely dissatisfied". Same `NA`-coding rules as health
satisfaction.

```{r}
#| label: life-sat
table(outcomes$sclfsato, useNA = "ifany")
# first, checking values of LS measure before changing
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  rename(life_sat = sclfsato) %>%
  mutate(life_sat = case_when(
    life_sat %in% c(-10, -9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
    #
    TRUE ~ 8 - as.numeric(life_sat)))
table(outcomes$life_sat, useNA = "ifany") # 43203 missing
```

### Financial situation (`finnow`)

This question asks individuals to rate their *current* subjective
financial situation, which we are referring to as "financial situation".

Rated on a scale of 1–5, with 1 being "living comfortably" and 5 being
"finding it very difficult".

```{r}
#| label: finnow
table(outcomes$finnow, useNA = "ifany")
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(finnow = case_when(
    finnow %in% c(-9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(finnow)
  ))
table(outcomes$finnow, useNA = "ifany") # 2207 missing
```

### Financial outlook (`finfut`)

This question asks individuals to rate their *future* subjective
financial situation a year from now, which we are referring to as
"financial outlook".

Original scale does 1–3, with 1 being "better off" and 2 being "worse
off" and 3 being about the same. I will be changing it to a rating where
1 is still "better off", but it is incrementally worse, so 2 = "about
the same" and 3 = "worse off".

```{r}
#| label: finfut
table(outcomes$finfut, useNA = "ifany")
outcomes <- outcomes %>%
  mutate(finfut = case_when(
    finfut %in% c(-9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
    finfut == 1 ~ 1,
    finfut == 2 ~ 3,
    finfut == 3 ~ 2,
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(finfut)
  ))
table(outcomes$finfut, useNA = "ifany") # can confirm switch went well, 11148 missing
```

### Simplifying outcome dataset and merging back into analytic sample

After all the outcomes have been cleaned and created, I wanted to
simplify the outcome dataset to just the cleaned variables needed, but
keeping original `outcomes` df if needed. Also, this step renames the
self-rated health question from `scsf1_combined`, which was created
above.

```{r}
#| label: outcomes-clean
outcomes_clean <- outcomes %>%
  rename(general_health = scsf1_combined) %>%
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, GHQ_total, SF_total, general_health, health_sat, life_sat, finnow, finfut)
# "outcomes" contains 532834 obs of 10 vars
```

```{r}
#| label: outcomes-merge
# adding cleaned vars back in
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  left_join(outcomes_clean, by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename"))
# keeping only those with valid GHQ data
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  filter(!is.na(GHQ_total))
# "UKHLS_analytic" contains 68519 obs of 25 vars
```

## Sociodemographic data

Variables I am going to clean here: age, sex, year of birth, ethnicity,
UK-born, religious affiliation.

-   Age (continuous): `age_dv` from `indall`
-   Sex (for face validity): `sex_dv` from `indall`
-   Year of birth: `doby_dv` from `indall`
-   Ethnicity (creating categories): `ethn_dv` from `indall`
-   UK-born (binary): `ukborn` from `indresp`
-   Religious affiliation: `oprlg1` from `indresp`
-   Urbanicity: `urban_dv` from `indresp`
-   De facto marital status: `mastat_dv` from `indresp`
-   Highest education level: `hiqual_dv` from `indresp`

```{r}
#| label: demo-init
ind_demo <- UKHLS_total %>%
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, age_dv, sex_dv, doby_dv, ethn_dv, oprlg1, urban_dv, hiqual_dv, mastat_dv, single_dv)
# "ind_demo" contains 532834 obs of 12 variables
```

### Age (`age`) (time-varying)

```{r}
#| label: demo-age
# age - time-varying
table(ind_demo$age_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 39 missing, also 28 15-year-olds, not sure if it's correct
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%
  rename(age = age_dv) %>%
  mutate(age = case_when(
    age == -9 ~ NA_real_, # missing
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(age)
    ))
table(ind_demo$age, useNA = "ifany") # 39 missing
```

### Sex (`sex`) (time-invariant for this study)

Sex (male = 1, female = 2), setting other values to NA. Time-invariant
for purposes of this study, so taking only first response.

```{r}
#| label: demo-sex
table(ind_demo$sex_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 10 missing (-9), 28 "inconsistent"
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%
  rename(sex = sex_dv) %>%
  arrange(pidp, wavename) %>%
  group_by(pidp) %>%
  mutate(
    sex_clean = case_when(
      sex == -9 ~ NA_real_, # missing
      sex == 0 ~ NA_real_, # inconsistent
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(sex)
    ),
    sex = first(na.omit(sex_clean))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-sex_clean)
table(ind_demo$sex, useNA = "ifany") # 1 = 236565, 2 = 296237, NA = 32
```

### Year of birth (`yob`) (time-varying)

For month/day of birth, we would have needed to request special
permission, so I am only including year here

```{r}

# year of birth (yob) - time-varying
table(ind_demo$doby_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 39 missing
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%
  rename(yob = doby_dv) %>%
  mutate(yob = case_when(

    TRUE ~ as.numeric(yob)
  ))
table(ind_demo$yob, useNA = "ifany") # 39 missing
```

### Ethnicity (`ethn` & `ethn_binary`) (time-invariant)

Ethnicity is time-invariant, so taking first available response. I am
also creating a new column titled `ethn_binary` because there might be
underpowering for conducting subgroup analyses at each ethnic category:

-   0 = White (from British/English/Scottish/Welsh/Northern Irish,
    Irish, Gypsy or Irish Traveller, any other White background — codes
    1–4)
-   1 = all others
-   Only `-9` should be present, not any of the other codings

```{r}
#| label: demo-ethnicity
# checking OG category breakdown - could see 
table(ind_demo$ethn_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 398 missing
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%
  rename(ethn = ethn_dv) %>%
  arrange(pidp, wavename) %>%
  group_by(pidp) %>%
  mutate(
    ethn_clean = case_when(
      ethn == -9 ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(ethn)
    ),
    ethn = first(na.omit(ethn_clean))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-ethn_clean) %>%
  mutate(ethn_binary = case_when(
    is.na(ethn) ~ NA_real_,
    ethn %in% c(1:2, 4) ~ 0, # white
    TRUE ~ 1 # non-white
  ))
table(ind_demo$ethn, useNA = "ifany")
table(ind_demo$ethn_binary, useNA = "ifany") # still 398 "missing"
# "ind_demo" contains 532834 obs of 13 variables
```

### UK-born (`ukborn`) (time-invariant)

Retrieving this actually from `xwavedat` because the `indresp` `ukborn`
variable was a proxy. Time-invariant, and only one answer already
present. (Note: `table(ind_demo$ukborn, useNA = "ifany")` would show 1–5
= born in UK.)

```{r}
#| label: demo-ukborn
# retrieve data from xwavedat file, then link by person
xwavedat <- read.delim("UKDA-6614-tab/tab/ukhls/xwavedat.tab", header = TRUE, sep = "\t", quote = "")
ukborn <- xwavedat %>%
  select(pidp, bornuk_dv)
table(ukborn$bornuk_dv, useNA = "ifany") # 1 = born in UK, 2 = not born in UK, -9 = missing
ukborn <- ukborn %>%
  rename(ukborn = bornuk_dv) %>%
  mutate(ukborn = case_when(
    ukborn == -9 ~ NA_real_, # missing
    TRUE ~ as.numeric(ukborn)
  ))
# merging ukborn back into ind_demo (since it's from a different data source)
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%

table(ind_demo$ukborn, useNA = "ifany") # 9082 missing
```

### Religious affiliation (`religion`) (time-invariant)

Time-invariant, so only collecting first valid response. Codes from
USOC:

-   `-8` (inapplicable), `-7` (proxy), `-2` (refusal), `-1` (don't know)
-   2 (Church of England/Anglican), 3 (Roman Catholic), 4 (Church of
    Scotland), 5 (Free Church or Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland),
    6 (Episcopalian), 7 (Methodist), 8 (Baptist), 9
    (Congregational/United Reform), 10 (other Christian), 11 (Christian
    — no specific denomination), 12 (Muslim/Islam), 13 (Hindu), 14
    (Jewish), 15 (Sikh), 16 (Buddhist), 17 (Church of Wales), 97 (other)

Grouping into 1 = Christian, 2 = Muslim, 3 = Hindu, 4 = other (based on
including criteria of 1% or more for category from [UK ARDA
profile](https://www.thearda.com/world-religion/national-profiles?u=233c#IRFDEMOG)).
Agnostic/Atheist isn't really feasible here.

```{r}
#| label: demo-religion
table(ind_demo$oprlg1, useNA = "ifany") # 23 missing, but 96.58% inapplicable -- too underpowered?
ind_demo <- ind_demo %>%
  rename(religion = oprlg1) %>%
  arrange(pidp, wavename) %>%
  group_by(pidp) %>%
  mutate(
    religion_clean = case_when(
      religion %in% c(-9, -8, -7, -2, -1) ~ NA_real_,
      religion %in% c(2:11, 17) ~ 1, # Christian
      religion == 12 ~ 2, # Muslim
      religion == 13 ~ 3, # Hindu
      religion %in% c(14:16, 97) ~ 4, # Other
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(religion)
    ),
    religion = first(na.omit(religion_clean))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-religion_clean)
table(ind_demo$religion, useNA = "ifany") # only 233040 missing - if wanted to, could try to use ff_ variable but tbd
```

Highest educational qualification ever reported, pulling from

### De facto marital status (`marstat`) (time-varying)

`2` (married), `3` (same-sex civil partnership), `4` (separated but
legally married), `5` (divorced), `6` (widowed), `7` (separated from
civil partner), `8` (former civil partner), `9` (former civil partner

Grouping into: 1 = single, 2 = partnered, 3 =
divorced/separated/widowed.

## Economic confounders

These are confounders including household income, income quintile, and
occupation class, as well as deriving equivalised income variables from
this. Relevant variables include:

-   `fihhmnnet1_dv` — total net household income (no deductions),
    derived net monthly
-   `ieqmoecd_dv` — modified OECD equivalence scale
-   `jbnssec3_dv` — current NS-SEC occupation class, derived (3 class
    version) (also retrieving `jlnssec3_dv`, the occupation class from
    last job - but since that's not as directly relevant I may not
    actually end up using it)

All counfounders from this section are considered time-varying.

Also, Needing to include `intdaty_dv` → `intyear`

```{r}
#| label: econ-init
ind_econ <- UKHLS_total %>%
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, intdaty_dv, fihhmnnet1_dv, ieqmoecd_dv, jbnssec3_dv, jlnssec3_dv)
# "ind_econ" contains 532834 obs of 8 vars 
```

**Inspecting household income variables**

```{r}
#| label: econ-income-inspect
# cleaning household vars
# household income
table(is.na(ind_econ$fihhmnnet1_dv)) # no missing
table(is.na(ind_econ$ieqmoecd_dv)) # no missing
```

### Equivalised household income (`equiv_monthly` and `equiv_yearly`)

I wanted to create a composite household income variable, dividing total
net monthly income by equivalence scale, and also converting it to a
yearly equivalised income, in order to use this as a household
equivalised income variable.

Creating equivalised household income variable from the two variables
provided:

-   `fihhmnnet1_dv`: total net household income (no deductions), derived
    net monthly
-   `ieqmoecd_dv`: modified OECD equivalence scale (need to set `-9` to
    NA first)

```{r}
#| label: econ-equivalised
ind_econ <- ind_econ %>%
  mutate(equiv_monthly = case_when(
    ieqmoecd_dv > 0 ~ fihhmnnet1_dv / ieqmoecd_dv,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_ # in case of invalid equivalence scale
  )) %>%
  mutate(equiv_yearly = equiv_monthly * 12)
summary(ind_econ$equiv_monthly) # 516 "NAs"
hist(ind_econ$equiv_monthly)
summary(ind_econ$equiv_yearly)
# "ind_econ" contains 532834 obs of 10 vars
```

**Merge `equiv_monthly` and `equiv_yearly` into analytic sample**

```{r}
#| label: econ-merge-income
# merging back into analytic sample to then calculate the quintiles/deciles
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  left_join(ind_econ %>% select(pidp, hidp, wavename, equiv_monthly, equiv_yearly), 
            by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename"))
# "UKHLS_analytic" contains 68537 obs of 37 vars
```

### Income quintiles and deciles (by year) (`income_quintile` and `income_decile`)

Create income quintiles and deciles using equiv_yearly income (although
note, this will have to be recalculated after imputation since you'll
have imputed values to consider anyway).

```{r}
#| label: econ-quintiles
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  group_by(intyear) %>%
  mutate(
    # quintiles (5ths) - for stratified analyses
    income_quintile = ntile(equiv_yearly, 5),
    # deciles (10ths) - for descriptives
    income_decile = ntile(equiv_yearly, 10)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
# "UKHLS_analytic" contains 68537 obs of 39 vars
```


### Occupation class (NS-SEC) (`oc_current`)

NS-SEC coding, should be derived. Including long-term unemployed
category (= 4) and short-term unemployed category (= 5); may have to
code inapplicable as inapplicable, missing as missing for these
variables. Coded as time-varying.

Current 3-class occupational category:

-   1 = management and professional,
-   2 = intermediate,
-   3 = routine and manual,
-   -8 = inapplicable (not employed)
-   -9 = missing

Grouped now into the following:

-   1 = management and professional,
-   2 = intermediate,
-   3 = routine and manual,
-   4 = long-term unemployed (having responded "inapplicable" to 3 or
    more waves)
-   5 = short-term unemployed (having responded "inapplicable" to \<3
    waves)
-   NA = missing

```{r}
#| label: econ-occupation
table(ind_econ$jbnssec3_dv, useNA = "ifany")
ind_econ <- ind_econ %>%
  rename(oc_current = jbnssec3_dv) %>%
  arrange(pidp, wavename) %>%
  group_by(pidp) %>%
  mutate(
    # clean the variable
    oc_clean = case_when(
      oc_current == -9 ~ NA_real_,  # missing
      oc_current == -8 ~ -8,  # inapplicable (not employed)
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(oc_current)
    ),
    # count consecutive unemployment spells
    is_unemployed = (oc_clean == -8),
    # create spell ID for consecutive unemployment
    unemploy_spell = cumsum(!is_unemployed | is.na(is_unemployed)),
    # count length of each unemployment spell
    unemploy_length = sequence(rle(is_unemployed)$lengths),
    # mark as long-term unemployed if 3+ consecutive waves
    is_longterm_unemployed = (is_unemployed & unemploy_length >= 3),
    # final coding
    oc_current = case_when(
      oc_clean > 0 ~ oc_clean,  # Has occupation
      is_longterm_unemployed ~ 4,  # 3+ waves unemployed
      oc_clean == -8 ~ 5,  # Short-term unemployment/not employed
      TRUE ~ NA_real_  # Missing only for -9
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(-oc_clean, -is_unemployed, -unemploy_spell, -unemploy_length, -is_longterm_unemployed)
table(ind_econ$oc_current, useNA = "ifany") # 106640 NA
```

**Merging occupation back into analytic sample**

```{r}
#| label: econ-merge-occupation
UKHLS_analytic <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  left_join(ind_econ %>% select(pidp, hidp, wavename, oc_current), 
            by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename"))
# "UKHLS_analytic" contains 68518 obs of 41 vars
```

### Chronic health (`chron_health`)

This is a long-standing health variable indicating the presence or
absence of a certain condition.

Note that not every one of these will be present across every wave. I
decided against using the `health` variable because it contains "mental
impairment, illness or disability" as part of the question, and that
could be overlapping with the mental health outcome, instead, I am
creating composite variable as described above.

From meeting with Jen Dykxhoorn about this, I figured that for health
variables, I will need to use loop/feed-forward function for
missing/inapplicable, as once individuals have indicated they have that
condition, they are not asked again. Also, not all health variables are
present at every wave, so will need to use most recent wave available.

Legend for checking distribution below: `-9` (missing), `-8`
(inapplicable), `-7` (proxy), `-2` (refusal), `-1` (don't know), 0 (not
mentioned), 1 (yes mentioned).

**Building composite chronic-health variable**

To set up this variable, I'm using `data.table` as that syntax is
faster.

```{r}
#| label: health-cond-setup
# chronic condition variables
setDT(ind_health)
cond_vars <- c(
  "hcond1","hcond2","hcond3","hcond4","hcond5","hcond6",
  "hcond7","hcond8","hcond9","hcond10","hcond11","hcond12",
  "hcond13","hcond14","hcond15","hcond16","hcond18","hcond19",
  "hcond21","hcond23","hcond24","hcond26","hcond27","hcond28",
  "hcond29"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: health-cond-recode
# recoding all condition variables (1=yes, 0=no, else NA)
ind_health[, (cond_vars) := lapply(.SD, function(x) fifelse(x == 1, 1, fifelse(x == 0, 0, NA_real_))), 
           .SDcols = cond_vars]
```

Forward filling ALL observations for each person (not just flagged
ones), just in case flag variable doesn't capture previous responses.

```{r}
#| label: health-cond-locf
ind_health[, (cond_vars) := lapply(.SD, function(x) nafill(x, type = "locf")), 
           by = pidp, .SDcols = cond_vars]
```

```{r}
#| label: health-cond-composite
# create composite with proper NA handling
ind_health[, chron_health := {
  has_any_data <- rowSums(!is.na(.SD)) > 0
  has_condition <- rowSums(.SD == 1, na.rm = TRUE) > 0
  fifelse(has_any_data, as.integer(has_condition), NA_integer_)
}, .SDcols = cond_vars]
table(ind_health$chron_health, useNA = "ifany")
```

```{r}
#| label: health-cond-check
table(ind_health$chron_health, useNA = "ifany") # 117627 NAs
# "ind_health" contains 532834 obs of 41 vars
```

This variable is similar to above, where I would mark an individual as

variable is being used after aggregating information from all the
different disability categories reported.

```{r}
# disdif4 = continence (bladder and bowel control)

# disdif5 = hearing (apart from using a standard hearing aid)
table(ind_health$disdif5, useNA = "ifany")
# disdif6 = sight (apart from wearing standard glasses)
table(ind_health$disdif6, useNA = "ifany")
# disdif7 = communication or speech problems
table(ind_health$disdif7, useNA = "ifany")
# disdif8 = memory or ability to concentrate, learn or understand
table(ind_health$disdif8, useNA = "ifany")
# disdif9 = recognising when you are in physical danger

```

**Building composite disability variable**

Again, as done above, using `data.table` as that syntax is faster.

```{r}
#| label: health-dis-setup
setDT(ind_health)
dis_vars <- c(
  "disdif1","disdif2","disdif3","disdif4","disdif5","disdif6",
  "disdif7","disdif8","disdif9","disdif10","disdif11","disdif12"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: health-dis-recode
# recoding disability variables (1=yes, 0=no, else NA)
ind_health[, (dis_vars) := lapply(.SD, function(x) fifelse(x == 1, 1, fifelse(x == 0, 0, NA_real_))), 
           .SDcols = dis_vars]
```

```{r}
#| label: health-dis-wave-indicator
# creating wave-level disability indicator
ind_health[, disability_wave := {
  has_any_data <- rowSums(!is.na(.SD)) > 0
  has_disability <- rowSums(.SD == 1, na.rm = TRUE) > 0
  fifelse(has_any_data, as.integer(has_disability), NA_integer_)
}, .SDcols = dis_vars]
```

Forwarding persistence after first disability (by person), and only
propagating `1` forward if there's ever a disability reported.

```{r}
#| label: health-dis-persistence
ind_health[, disability := {
  if (any(disability_wave == 1, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    cummax(replace(disability_wave, is.na(disability_wave), 0))
  } else {
    disability_wave  # Keep NAs if never reported disability
  }
}, by = pidp]
```

```{r}
#| label: health-dis-cleanup
# cleaning up
ind_health[, disability_wave := NULL]

table(ind_health$disability, useNA = "ifany") # 132445 NAs
# "ind_health" contains 532834 obs of 42 vars
```

```{r}
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, chron_health, disability)

```

```{r}

  inner_join(ind_health_composite, by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename"))
```

## Obtaining missingness information (pre-imputation)

### Missingness summary table

First, we'll create a missingness summary table BEFORE imputation, only
including outcomes, exposure/treatment, and covariates.

Here I extract the relevant variables:

```{r}
#| label: vars-to-check
vars_to_check <- c(
  # outcomes
  "GHQ_total", "SF_total", "general_health", "health_sat", "life_sat", "finnow", "finfut",
  # exposure/treatment variables
  "family_3plus", "treated", "age_youngest_child", "n_children_5_under",
  # covariates to be imputed
  "age", "sex", "ethn_binary", "ukborn", "urban", 
  "edu_qual", "marstat", "equiv_yearly", "income_quintile",
  "oc_current", "chron_health", "religion", "disability"
)
```

Then, I create a missingness table with all missing values for the
variables included above.

```{r}
#| label: missingness-summary
missingness_summary <- UKHLS_analytic %>%
  select(all_of(vars_to_check)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), 
                   ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "Variable", 
               values_to = "Missing_n") %>%
  mutate(
    Total_n = nrow(UKHLS_analytic),
    Missing_percent = round((Missing_n / Total_n) * 100, 2),
    Complete_n = Total_n - Missing_n,
    Complete_percent = round((Complete_n / Total_n) * 100, 2)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing_percent)) %>%
  select(Variable, Total_n, Complete_n, Complete_percent, Missing_n, Missing_percent)
print(missingness_summary, n = Inf)
```

Also exporting this table as an Excel file in case I'd want to make a
table or see the exported version as reference!

```{r}
#| label: missingness-export
# exporting missingness table
write.csv(missingness_summary, "missingness_table_pre_20260220.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Also, at this stage, upon seeing the output, we decided not to impute
religion (48.5% missingness) or disability (37.4% missingness) anymore
bc of \>30% missingness.

### Quick total missing cells tabulation

As per Praveetha, we figured it would be worth having a rough estimate
of how many cells were missing, to see the levels of imputation
potentially needed.

```{r}
#| label: total-missing-cells

sum(is.na(UKHLS_analytic_full)) # 112022
# total cells in dataset
nrow(UKHLS_analytic_full) * ncol(UKHLS_analytic_full) # 3014792
# percentage missing
percent_missing <- (sum(is.na(UKHLS_analytic_full)) / 
                      (nrow(UKHLS_analytic_full) * ncol(UKHLS_analytic_full))) * 100
percent_missing # 3.72%
```

### Missingness per outcome calculation

We then figured it made sense to obtain a similar proportion to above,
but counting missingness and completeness for each outcome.

```{r}
#| label: outcome-check-build
outcome_check <- UKHLS_analytic_full %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    
    GHQ_complete = sum(!is.na(GHQ_total)),
    GHQ_missing = sum(is.na(GHQ_total)),
    GHQ_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(GHQ_total)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    SF_complete = sum(!is.na(SF_total)),
    SF_missing = sum(is.na(SF_total)),
    SF_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(SF_total)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    general_health_complete = sum(!is.na(general_health)),
    general_health_missing = sum(is.na(general_health)),
    general_health_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(general_health)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    health_sat_complete = sum(!is.na(health_sat)),
    health_sat_missing = sum(is.na(health_sat)),
    health_sat_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(health_sat)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    life_sat_complete = sum(!is.na(life_sat)),
    life_sat_missing = sum(is.na(life_sat)),
    life_sat_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(life_sat)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    finnow_complete = sum(!is.na(finnow)),
    finnow_missing = sum(is.na(finnow)),
    finnow_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(finnow)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    finfut_complete = sum(!is.na(finfut)),
    finfut_missing = sum(is.na(finfut)),
    finfut_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(finfut)) / n() * 100, 2)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: outcome-check-print
# viewing as a nice table
outcome_check %>% 
  pivot_longer(-n_total) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

### Missingness per exposure variable calculation

Counting missing and complete for each exposure variable.

```{r}
#| label: exposure-check-build
exposure_check <- UKHLS_analytic_full %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    
    family_3plus_complete = sum(!is.na(family_3plus)),
    family_3plus_missing = sum(is.na(family_3plus)),
    family_3plus_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(family_3plus)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    treated_complete = sum(!is.na(treated)),
    treated_missing = sum(is.na(treated)),
    treated_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(treated)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    time_bucket_complete = sum(!is.na(time_bucket)),
    time_bucket_missing = sum(is.na(time_bucket)),
    time_bucket_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(time_bucket)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    post_policy_month_complete = sum(!is.na(post_policy_month)),
    post_policy_month_missing = sum(is.na(post_policy_month)),
    post_policy_month_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(post_policy_month)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    age_youngest_child_complete = sum(!is.na(age_youngest_child)),
    age_youngest_child_missing = sum(is.na(age_youngest_child)),
    age_youngest_child_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(age_youngest_child)) / n() * 100, 2),
    
    n_children_5_under_complete = sum(!is.na(n_children_5_under)),
    n_children_5_under_missing = sum(is.na(n_children_5_under)),
    n_children_5_under_pct_complete = round(sum(!is.na(n_children_5_under)) / n() * 100, 2)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: exposure-check-print

exposure_check %>% 
  pivot_longer(-n_total) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
```

## Imputation setup and implementation

### Preparing data for imputation

In order to prepare the data for imputation, I am trying to keep model
more minimal for now.

```{r}
#| label: imp-prepare-df
df <- UKHLS_analytic_full %>%
  select(
    # ID variables (don't impute)
    pidp, hidp, wavename,
    # exposure variables (don't impute)
    age_youngest_child, n_children_5_under, family_3plus, treated, time_bucket, post_policy_month, intyear, 
    # outcomes (now imputing these)
    GHQ_total, SF_total, general_health, health_sat, life_sat, finnow, finfut,
    # confounders (DO impute) - matches variables in feols() models
    age, sex, ethn_binary, ukborn, urban, 
    edu_qual, marstat, equiv_yearly,
    oc_current, chron_health
  )
df <- df %>% select(where(~ !all(is.na(.x))))
# "df" contains 68518 obs of 27 variables
```

### Initialising MICE

The kind of imputation I'll be using here is multiple imputation using
chained equations (MICE). I first set up the MICE and check if there are
any logged events (potential problems with data and what corrective
action MICE took).

```{r}
#| label: imp-init
# initialising MICE
ini <- mice(df, maxit = 0, print = FALSE)
meth <- ini$method
pred <- ini$predictorMatrix
```

```{r}
#| label: imp-logged-events
# check what the logged events are
ini$loggedEvents # "hidp" and "treated" are removed from imputation due to collinearity
```

### Set imputation method and predictor matrix

Since we are not imputing ID variable(s) or exposure-related variables,
I am making that distinction clear.

```{r}
#| label: imp-dont-impute
dont_impute <- c(
  "pidp", "hidp", "wavename",
  "age_youngest_child", "n_children_5_under", "family_3plus", 
  "treated", "time_bucket", "post_policy_month", "intyear"
)

for(v in dont_impute) {
  if(v %in% names(meth)) {
    meth[v] <- ""
    pred[, v] <- 1
  }
}
```

Not using ID variables as predictors (as they're just labels, not
substantive predictors).

```{r}
#| label: imp-id-not-predictors
pred[, "pidp"] <- 0
pred[, "hidp"] <- 0
pred[, "wavename"] <- 0
```

Using single-level predictive-mean-matching (PMM) for all variables to
be imputed, as household clustering is still accounted for in analysis
(`feols` models use `cluster = ~hidp`).

```{r}
#| label: imp-method-pmm
for(v in names(meth)) {
  if(meth[v] == "") next
  meth[v] <- "pmm"
}
```

### Test run

I've commented it out in this code, but if you wanted to run a test
first, I've set the following parameters for this test run:

-   `m=2`: generating two datasets

-   `maxit=5`: algorithm runs five iterations

Diagnostics checked via `plot(imp_test)`, `stripplot(imp_test)`, and
`densityplot(imp_test)`.

```{r}
#| label: imp-test-run
# test run first: m=2, maxit=5
# imp_test <- mice(df, m = 2, maxit = 5, method = meth, 
#                 predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 123, print = TRUE)

# check diagnostic
# plot(imp_test)
# stripplot(imp_test)
# densityplot(imp_test)
```

### Full imputation

If test looks good, run full imputation: `m = 20` (doing this because of
interaction terms), `maxit = 10` (because the convergence plots were
still looking a bit unstable at `maxit = 5`). This can be quite heavy
computationally, so be careful!

```{r}
#| label: imp-full-run
imp <- mice(df, m = 20, maxit = 10, method = meth, 
            predictorMatrix = pred, seed = 123, print = TRUE)
```

Once the plot has been run, plotting convergence plots for visual
inspection.

```{r}
#| label: imp-convergence-plot
pdf("output/mice_convergence_plots_20260220.pdf", width = 10, height = 8)
plot(imp)
dev.off()
```

Now saving full imputed object – **instead of running the imputation
each time, you should reload this object after you've done imputation!**

```{r}
#| label: imp-save-object
# save imputation object (all 20 datasets)
saveRDS(imp, "UKHLS_imputation_object_20260220.rds")
imp$loggedEvents # one logged event that was collinear -- treated variable removed from predictors bc it was collinear with other variables
```

### Imputation diagnostics (and troubleshooting if necessary)

First, verifying the number of NAs for all imputed variables - should
see zero.

```{r}
#| label: imp-verify-no-na
imp_missing <- complete(imp, "long") %>%  # Stacks all 20 datasets
  group_by(.imp) %>%  # Group by imputation number
  summarise(across(c(age, sex, ethn_binary, ukborn, urban, 
                     edu_qual, marstat, equiv_yearly, oc_current, 
                     chron_health, GHQ_total, SF_total, general_health, 
                     health_sat, life_sat, finnow, finfut), 
                   ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  print(n = Inf)
# Or print to console without truncation
print(imp_missing, width = Inf)
```

observations with any remaining NAs from dataset 1 (because the
missingness pattern will be the same across all datasets).

```{r}
#                  health_sat, life_sat, finnow, finfut),

# view them
```

### Post-imputation data management

First, stack all datasets (including original) for manipulation
purposes. Using `include = TRUE` so we get datasets 0–20.

```{r}
#| label: imp-stack-long
imp_long <- complete(imp, "long", include = TRUE)  # WITH include=TRUE (datasets 0-20)
```

Now, add unimputed exposure variables back to all datasets:

```{r}
#| label: imp-add-exposure-back
time_vars <- UKHLS_analytic_full %>%
  select(pidp, hidp, wavename, intmonth, intym, 
         n_children_u18, any_third_plus_post_policy,
         youngest_5_under, time_since_policy, third_child_yob)
imp_long <- imp_long %>%
  left_join(time_vars, by = c("pidp", "hidp", "wavename"))
```

Remember earlier how I'd mentioned we'd need to recalculate income
quintiles for all datasets since you have different values now? Here's
where we can do that:

```{r}
#| label: imp-recalc-quintiles
imp_long <- imp_long %>%
  group_by(.imp, intyear) %>%  # group by imputation and year
  mutate(
    income_quintile = ntile(equiv_yearly, 5),
    income_decile = ntile(equiv_yearly, 10)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

**Create z-score standardisation for outcomes**

Highlighting this step as it's incredibly important - these outcomes
will be the ones used for our analyses, and the plan is to report both
raw and standardised outcomes. Standardising within each imputed
dataset.

```{r}
#| label: imp-zscore-outcomes
imp_long <- imp_long %>%
  group_by(.imp) %>%  # standardising within each imputed dataset
  mutate(
    GHQ_total_z = scale(GHQ_total)[,1],
    SF_total_z = scale(SF_total)[,1],
    general_health_z = scale(general_health)[,1],
    health_sat_z = scale(health_sat)[,1],
    life_sat_z = scale(life_sat)[,1],
    finnow_z = scale(finnow)[,1],
    finfut_z = scale(finfut)[,1]
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```

**Saving `imp_long` and `imp_complete` datasets**

You'll need both versions, because depending on the kind of analysis
you're doing (descriptive or inferential statistics), you'll be using
one or the other.

For reference:

-   `imp_long` - contains all 20 datasets, put together one after the
    other

-   `imp_complete` - contains imputation object with all 20 datasets

```{r}
#| label: imp-save-long
saveRDS(imp_long, "UKHLS_imputation_long_20260220.rds")
# "imp_long" contains 1438878 obs of 45 vars
```

```{r}
#| label: imp-back-to-mids
imp_complete <- as.mids(imp_long)

# save imputation objects (all datasets)
saveRDS(imp_complete, "UKHLS_imputation_sets_20260220.rds")
```

# Section 4: descriptives and analysis

Now we can run the full sample analyses on the prepared dataset for
policy evaluation.

You'll be using metadata vectors which will be referred to throughout

```{r}
#| label: outcome-metadata-vectors-defined-here-fo
# outcome metadata vectors - defined here for use throughout script
outcomes_raw   <- c("GHQ_total", "SF_total", "general_health", "health_sat", "life_sat", "finnow", "finfut")
outcome_labels <- c("GHQ-12", "SF-12", "General Health", "Health Sat", "Life Sat", "Fin Now", "Fin Future")
```

This is currently still in the old order and labelling from before we
decided to group the outcomes in the current way
(mental/general/financial health), so I am adding a command to make sure
the ordering gets updated and changed, and I am adding a vector here
which will use said updated labelling. of the study. As a reminder, the
labels used correspond to the following outcomes:

-   `GHQ_total` -\> **psychological distress**

-   `SF_total` -\> **health-related quality of life (HRQoL)**

-   `general_health` -\> **self-rated health**

-   `health_sat` -\> **health satisfaction**

-   `life_sat` -\> **life satisfaction**

-   `finnow` -\> **financial situation**

-   `finfut` -\> **financial outlook**

After this command below is run, the ordering for exported
tables/figures will be as follows:

-   psychological distress

-   life satisfaction

-   self-rated health

-   health-related quality of life (HRQoL)

-   health satisfaction

-   financial situation

-   financial outlook

This order is now consistent with the groupings above on **mental
health** (psychological distress, life satisfaction), **general health**
(self-rated health, HRQoL, and health satisfaction), and **financial
health** (financial situation, financial outlook). Unfortunately, with
the magnitude of code, it would be very difficult to go into each model
and change the ordering here, so I've kept the raw code ordering for the
models as-is. Just note that when it's exported, the new labels and
ordering apply.

```{r}
#| label: display-reordering-ghq-life-sat-general
# display reordering: GHQ, life_sat, general_health, SF, health_sat, finnow, finfut
# (maps from original positions to new display positions)
display_order <- c(1, 5, 3, 2, 4, 6, 7)
# figure-specific labels (in ORIGINAL variable order — reordered via display_order when plotting)
outcome_labels_figures <- c(
  "Psychological Distress",              # GHQ_total      (position 1)
  "Health-Related Quality of Life",      # SF_total        (position 2)
  "Self-Rated Health",                   # general_health  (position 3)
  "Health Satisfaction",                 # health_sat      (position 4)
  "Life Satisfaction",                   # life_sat        (position 5)
  "Financial Situation",                 # finnow          (position 6)
  "Financial Outlook"                    # finfut          (position 7)
)
```

```{r}

# y-axis labels (parentheticals indicate higher = worse direction for reverse-coded outcomes)
outcome_ylabs_figures <- c(
  "Psychological Distress",              # GHQ_total      (position 1) — higher = more distress, no qualifier needed
  "(Worse) Health-Related Quality of Life", # SF_total     (position 2) — higher = worse HRQoL
  "(Lower) Self-Rated Health",           # general_health  (position 3) — higher = lower health
  "(Lower) Health Satisfaction",         # health_sat      (position 4) — higher = lower satisfaction
  "(Lower) Life Satisfaction",           # life_sat        (position 5) — higher = lower satisfaction
  "(Worse) Financial Situation",         # finnow          (position 6) — higher = worse finances
  "(Worse) Financial Outlook"            # finfut          (position 7) — higher = worse outlook
)
```
